sections.html:
• Other names: Cone shell hermit crab, Striped hermit crab, Orange legged hermit
  • Minimum tank size: 15 gallons (~60 litres)
  • Breeding: very difficult
  • Water type: SG 1.020–1.025
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: omnivore/carnivore
  • Temperament: semi-aggressive
  • Colour: red, orange and white

Halloween hermit crabs are widely distributed in the Indo-West Pacific, including the Red Sea, the west coast of India, Sri Lanka, the NW Australian coast, Vietnam, Indonesia, Taiwan, southern Japan, the Philippines, the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam, Papua New Guinea, eastern Australia and Hawaii.

Ciliopagurus strigatus is the most common species of the genus Ciliopagurus in the world. They are typically found in the low intertidal zone or shallow waters (5–15 m), especially along sandy areas around reefs.

Provide a tank of at least 15 gallons (~60 litres) per adult Halloween hermit crab you plan to house. More important than tank size is making sure the tank is completely cycled before introducing any Halloween hermit crab.

Halloween hermit crabs are fairly easy to care for and are considered low maintenance across the board, because they are very adaptable and do well in a range of water conditions.

Always have several extra empty shells available. In the wild, the need to find a new shell has driven Halloween hermit crabs to open hostility, with recorded instances of them attacking even snails or fighting each other for a larger or proper shell. Having shells of multiple sizes in the tank ensures the crab can easily find a new shell when the old one gets too small.

Unlike most hermit crabs, the Halloween hermit crab has a flattened body that allows it to use cone shells (Conus textile) with a narrow opening. Conus textile snails are carnivorous predators of other molluscs, and are among the most venomous creatures on earth, responsible for numerous fatalities worldwide. Never pick up cone shells on the beach: their proboscis can penetrate even a thin wetsuit and gloves. The venom causes intense pain, swelling, muscle paralysis and breathing failure.

Like all crustaceans, they must molt at regular intervals to grow. During this time the crab will try to hide until its new shell has hardened. After every molt, hermit crabs need larger shells; if they cannot find an empty one, they will actively fight over shells. Most metabolic activities are reduced during pre-molting, so if your crab does not eat as it used to, this can be a sign of molting.

Acclimate them before putting them in the tank.
For optimum growth, Halloween hermit crabs need a temperature of 22–28°C, pH 8.0–8.5, KH 8–16 and SG 1.020–1.025.

They prefer aquariums with live rock and a substrate they can sift through (such as sand or small gravel). They are nocturnal and often hide in or near the live rock when the lights are on.

They do not need fancy filtration and lighting; a normal LED aquarium light is enough.

Feeding is easy because they are omnivores and great scavengers. They will eat almost anything they find in the tank, including detritus, leftovers, dead organisms, green hair algae and so on. Their taste for algae means they naturally rid the aquarium of excess algae. However, do not assume that because they are scavengers they will take care of themselves; if underfed they become more aggressive.

Feed once or twice a week, for example raw table shrimp, frozen mysis shrimp, silversides, scallop, clam, mussel and algae tablets. If there is no algae in the tank, give algae tablets.

Halloween hermit crabs are nocturnal: they typically rest during the day and come out at night. They are generally active and always looking for food, though they sometimes spend long periods motionless inside the shell.

They are generally reef-safe. They will not eat corals, but because of their size they can accidentally knock them over or damage them. They spend most of their time on the substrate. To prevent incidents, some aquarists advise gluing corals to the rocks.

They are not necessarily the most docile animals and can turn hostile to other animals if not properly fed. Some aquarists reported hermit crabs catching small bottom-dwelling fish such as dragonets, firefish and some gobies. They can be described as semi-aggressive, so think carefully about tankmates and observe closely, as there are reports of occasional rogue individuals. Keeping them with decorative snails is risky; even with many spare empty shells, the risk of aggression remains.

When reproducing, male crabs can detect when females are fertile and then attach themselves to the female until the eggs are fertilised. The eggs stay on the underside of the female, inside her shell, until they hatch.

It is relatively difficult to breed them in captivity. Hermit crab larvae appear to have differing salinity needs, making captive breeding almost impossible.

Their legs are patterned with red and orange stripes. The flattened carapace is pure white and the abdomen is red with a pattern of undulating yellow lines. Their colouring is so distinctive that some consider it the brightest crustacean in home aquaria.

There are four hermit crabs of the genus Ciliopagurus that are morphologically very similar, and even biologists can separate them with confidence only by colouration: Ciliopagurus tricolor (blue leg hermit crab), Ciliopagurus galzini, Ciliopagurus vakovako and Ciliopagurus strigatus. All have similar patterns of transverse bands on the chelipeds and walking legs, but each can be recognised by the distinct colour and/or arrangement of these bands.

They tend to run on the larger side, growing up to 5 cm, larger than many other hermit crabs. According to different reports they can live 8–10 years in captivity.
